solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: USA's abandoned wise folk – they've been stuffed

indicators.note: abandoned can mean wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: the country's abbreviation, taken as written
sages are wise people

explanation.surface: A political jibe: America has abandoned its wise elders, who have been well and truly done for.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of USA's only joins the two parts. 'Stuffed' sounds like slang for defeated, but it is literal: sausages are skins stuffed with meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Sausages are made by filling a casing with minced meat, so they are things that have literally been filled up.

clue.text: Two versions of Cyclops recruited by politician Johnson for the battle

indicators.note: whoever is recruited is taken inside an organisation, so these letters go inside another word

blocks.note: Alan Johnson, Labour Home Secretary under Gordon Brown
the setter, Cyclops, can refer to himself in two ways: as object and as subject pronoun

explanation.surface: Two Private Eye setters are drafted by a Labour politician to fight a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Johnson is a British Labour politician; the surface wants you to think of Boris. A setter's name in his own clue stands for the first person, and 'two versions' asks for both the object and subject forms.
explanation.definitionFit: El Alamein in Egypt was the site of the decisive 1942 desert engagement between Montgomery's Eighth Army and Rommel.

clue.text: Cut down on corporal punishment (held up by a couple of tits?)

definitions.text: held up by a couple of tits?
definitions.note: an adjectival phrase with a question mark: the cheeky description of a garment with no shoulder straps

indicators.note: reducing something 'on' a thing means the reduction is applied to what follows, so the piece read first is sent to the back of the answer

blocks.note: a leather belt once used to beat pupils
to cut down on something is to have less of it, and the word follows what is reduced

explanation.surface: A call to reduce school beatings, with a schoolboy aside about birds.
explanation.walkthrough: Less strap is literally a cut in corporal punishment, so the words reverse order: STRAP + LESS. The tits in brackets are not birds but breasts, which hold up a dress without straps.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapless dress or bra has no shoulder support, so the wearer's bust is what keeps the garment in place.

clue.text: "Sacrifice Green's head!": morning piece

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
AM, ante meridiem, marks the morning hours
a bit is a piece of something

explanation.surface: A demand to sack Green, perhaps the Tory minister Damian Green, read as a morning newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacrifice ... head' looks like an order to sack someone, but 'Sacrifice' is the definition. Chess terms surface twice: a gambit sacrifices a piece, which the clue also uses.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess a gambit is an opening in which a pawn or piece is given up deliberately for positional advantage.

clue.text: Chary about conspiracy by Corbyn's no. 1 (rather patchy)

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps itself round the rest
number one is the first in line, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: chary and shy both mean wary or cautious
a plot is a conspiracy
the opening letter of the Labour leader's name

explanation.surface: Someone wary of a conspiracy theory about the Labour leader, whose record is rather patchy.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn led the Labour Party at the time. The wrapping word opens after its first letter, so the inserted pieces sit between its opening letter and the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something marked with irregular blots or smudges of colour is uneven in appearance, which is what patchy describes.

clue.text: (& 27ac.) Province following the PM? Not too clear, that

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase pointing back to the noun: 'that' is the thing which is not too clear

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece is placed second in the answer

blocks.note: Earl Grey was Prime Minister from 1830 to 1834; the question mark flags that it is one PM among many
a province is an area or region

explanation.surface: A question about which region follows the Prime Minister's lead, with the comment that it is all rather murky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The PM' makes you think of the current one, but it is the 19th-century Earl Grey. The province goes after him.
explanation.definitionFit: A grey area is a situation or subject where the rules are ill-defined, neither black nor white, so it is unclear.

clue.text: Age of Blair? Not quite, after e.g. reversal

indicators.note: the clue names the operation outright: these letters are turned round
not quite means just short of complete, so the final letter is dropped
after places this piece behind the other in the answer

blocks.note: the abbreviation for 'for example', taken as written
Tony Blair, Labour Prime Minister 1997-2007

explanation.surface: A query about the Blair era, followed by a note that something has been reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Age of Blair' reads as a noun, the Blair years, but 'Age' is a verb. The reversed abbreviation comes first, the shortened first name after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To get on is an idiom for growing older, so it matches the verb meaning to become elderly.

clue.text: Saying "Erdogan's top swine" and stuff

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of the Turkish president's name
a swine is a pig
to stuff is to cram or ram something in

explanation.surface: Someone quoting an insult about Turkey's president, Erdogan's top swine, and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And stuff' sounds like a vague 'et cetera', but 'stuff' is a verb meaning to pack in tightly.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a short, witty remark or pithy maxim, which is a kind of memorable saying.

clue.text: I fiddled with scanties, thus endlessly eager

indicators.note: fiddling with something messes it about, so the letters are rearranged
without an end, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; scanties are skimpy knickers
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A confession of messing with someone's knickers, out of overeager lust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddled with scanties' is innuendo; 'fiddled with' is the anagram signal acting on I, SCANTIES and the shortened THUS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Being eager means showing keen interest and excitement, which is a plain synonym for this adjective.

clue.text: Plan produced by heartless, beastly mother, confiscating sex rejuvenator, "very lacking"

indicators.note: without a heart, so the middle letter of the word is removed
to confiscate is to take and hold something, so one piece is held inside another
lacking means going without, so the letter named is taken out

blocks.note: a dam is the mother of an animal
the brand-name drug for erectile dysfunction
V is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: An outraged headline about a cruel mother seizing someone's Viagra, a plan that badly misfires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' sounds like a moral judgement but means 'of beasts', and 'very lacking' tells you the drug drops its V before it goes inside the heartless mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a drawing that shows the layout of something, as an architect's plan does.

clue.text: A warning that has Tory rebels going their separate way?

definitions.text: A warning that has Tory rebels going their separate way?

blocks.clueFragment: A warning that has Tory rebels going their separate way?
blocks.note: surface reading: an alarm that splits a rebellious party, sending its dissidents off on their own path
setter's reading: the Commons summons MPs to vote, and they physically part into the Aye and No lobbies

explanation.walkthrough: In the Commons a vote is a division: MPs walk through separate lobbies. A bell rings to call them, and rebels then go a different way from their whips.
explanation.definitionFit: The bell rung around Parliament gives members a few minutes' notice to reach the lobbies before a vote is taken.

clue.text: European's valiant "Out!"

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are put in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A brave European shouting for Britain to get out, a Brexit cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out!' looks like a Brexit slogan, but it only tells you to rearrange the brave word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latvian is a native of Latvia, a Baltic state that belongs to the EU, so is one kind of European.

clue.text: Eye has tip: "Angle"

blocks.note: to eye something is to view it
the tip of a pencil or knife is its point

explanation.surface: Private Eye has a tip-off, an angle on a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eye' looks like the magazine itself, but it is the verb to look at.
explanation.definitionFit: An angle on something is a particular way of looking at it, a perspective or standpoint.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Hooker ran off on receiving Trump's introduction – troublesome state!

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are rearranged
an introduction is the start of something, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the US President's name

explanation.surface: A prostitute fled on getting a visit from Trump, a troublesome business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooker ran off' reads as a story of a fleeing escort; 'off' is the anagram signal, and T joins the letters before they are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: North Korea, the nuclear-armed dictatorship led by Kim Jong-un, was a constant source of crisis for Trump's administration.

clue.text: Murdoch organ fixed – and so ends our enlightenment?

definitions.note: a phrase describing the event in question form; it stands for the noun as 'that which ends our light'

blocks.note: The Sun is Rupert Murdoch's British tabloid newspaper
set means fixed or firm

explanation.surface: A dig at the Murdoch press, rigged and the death of public understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enlightenment' suggests knowledge and reason; the setter means daylight, which ends when the sun goes down.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunset is when daylight fails each evening, so it literally brings an end to our natural illumination.

clue.text: see 21dn.
"Balls lifted – some sort of miracle!" (rhetorical type)

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting letters makes them read from the bottom upwards
a sort of something is a version of it, so the word appears in a different arrangement

blocks.note: Ed Balls, former Labour Shadow Chancellor
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaiming that a set of balls rising is a miracle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is a surname, not testicles or footballs: Ed Balls was a Labour minister, later on Strictly Come Dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A declaimer speaks in a grand oratorical style, so is a person given to rhetoric.

clue.text: Lobbies about 'old bags'

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: lobbies and halls are both entrance rooms
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lobbyists complaining about some old bags, which sounds like an insult to older women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bags' sounds like an insult, but the two words split: 'old' is fodder and 'bags' alone is the definition. The quote marks carry no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A holdall is a large soft bag for carrying clothes and belongings on a trip.

clue.text: Is smeared with cocoa at start of new party

indicators.note: smeared things are spread and messed about, so the letters are mixed up
the start of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone gets cocoa smeared on them at the start of a new political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New party' suggests a political launch; 'party' alone is the definition, and 'new' gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An occasion is a special event or celebration, and a party is one such social function.

clue.text: House of Commons kind of pot?

blocks.note: first meaning: a legislative assembly or the hall in which it sits
second meaning: the word that goes before 'pot' for a bedroom potty

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the second sense, which completes a compound rather than meaning pot by itself; the joke likens Parliament to a potty.
explanation.definitionFit: The Commons sits as a legislative chamber, and a chamber pot is a bowl kept under the bed for use at night.

clue.text: Drink that is maintaining Conservative line-up without May's lead

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold or keep, so one piece holds another inside it
a lead is the front position, so only the first letter is kept
without means lacking, so the named letter is taken away

blocks.note: i.e., the abbreviation for id est, meaning 'that is'
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
a team line-up is the selected side
the first letter of the Prime Minister's name

explanation.surface: A political sketch of Theresa May's Tory cabinet without her at its head.
explanation.walkthrough: Theresa May was Prime Minister when this appeared. The surface asks you to remove May from her team; only her first letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Iced tea, or ice tea, is chilled tea served as a cold drink, a common soft drink.

clue.text: Spin is ultimately bullshit and piss

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
widdle is a childish British word for urinate

explanation.surface: A verdict on political spin: it is all bullshit and piss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' looks like PR spin, which the surface damns; here it is the plain verb to turn something round.
explanation.definitionFit: To twiddle a knob or dial is to turn it idly back and forth, which is a way of rotating it.

clue.text: (& 14ac.) Miserable, rattled PM disowned Hunt

indicators.note: a rattled thing is shaken up, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy, flustered Prime Minister cuts loose Jeremy Hunt, her cabinet minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Hunt was in Theresa May's cabinet. 'Miserable' and 'rattled' both look like descriptions of the PM; only the first is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being down in the dumps is an idiom for feeling low and depressed, which is what an unhappy person is.

clue.text: Second-rate, flaccid? Ignore

blocks.note: B grade is second class
lank means limp or drooping

explanation.surface: A deflating verdict on a limp performance, best ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second-rate, flaccid' sounds like one insult; it is two pieces, a grade letter and a word for limp hair.
explanation.definitionFit: To blank someone is informal for snubbing them, refusing to acknowledge them when you meet.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Be suggestive and trendy in kinky hard top

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters are bent into a new order
the word in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: Fashion advice: flirt by wearing a fashionable kinky top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suggestive' hints at innuendo, as does 'kinky'; the trendy word goes inside the jumbled letters of HARD TOP.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop a hint is to suggest something indirectly, so it is to be suggestive in the plain sense.

clue.text: Progressive spewed bile at Republican vice president

indicators.note: spewed matter comes out in a mess, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for Republican
Al Gore was US Vice President under Clinton

explanation.surface: A progressive pours bile on Mike Pence, the Republican Vice President.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Republican vice president' points at Pence, but it is two pieces: R, then AL, from Al Gore, a Democrat, which the surface hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Progressive and liberal are both labels for left-of-centre politics favouring reform, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Unstable domain : country's leader is all over the place

indicators.note: something unstable will not stay in the order it is given
a leader goes first, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A shaky realm whose head of state is erratic and all over the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country's leader' sounds like a president; it means only the first letter of 'country'. 'All over the place' is a description of the leader in the surface but defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomadic people roam from place to place with no fixed home, so they are found everywhere in turn.

clue.text: see 6ac.
Sun: "Queen in lingerie", and miscellaneous items

indicators.note: the word in places one piece within the other

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for Sunday or sun
undies is informal for underwear
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline from The Sun about the Queen in her underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun:' reads as the newspaper reporting a scandal, but it gives only S. The Queen as R sits inside the underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundries are various small items too minor to list separately, which is exactly what miscellaneous things are.
